replacement: No, I can never forget those moments. She began telling her story. She told everything, the whole episode that Mitya had told Alyosha, her bowing to the ground, and her reason for it. She told about her father and how she went to Mitya. Not in one word, not in a single hint, did she let on that Mitya himself, through her sister, had suggested that they “send Katerina Ivanovna” to fetch the money. She generously kept that back, and she was not ashamed to make it seem that she had run to the young officer on her own impulse, counting on something ... to beg him for the money. It was something tremendous! I went cold and trembled as I listened. The court was hushed, straining to catch each word. It was something without precedent. Even from a girl as willful and scornfully proud as she was, such a frank confession, such sacrifice, such giving up of herself, seemed unbelievable. And for what, and for whom? To save the man who had deceived and insulted her, and to help, however little, in saving him, by making a strong impression in his favor. And indeed, the figure of the young officer who, with a respectful bow to the innocent girl, handed her his last four thousand roubles, all he had in the world, was cast in a very sympathetic and attractive light. But ... I had a painful misgiving in my heart! I felt that slander might come of it later (and it did, in fact, it did). All over town afterwards it was repeated, with spiteful laughter, that the story was perhaps not quite complete, that is, in the statement that the officer had let the young lady leave “with nothing but a respectful bow.” People hinted that something had been left out here.

This came as a complete surprise to everyone. Nobody in the town or the monastery, not even Mitya, had known it. I was told that Rakitin went purple with shame where he sat. Somehow Grushenka had heard, before she came into court, that he had testified against Mitya, and that was why she was angry. This time the whole effect on the public of Rakitin’s speech, of his noble sentiments and his attacks on serfdom and on the political disorder of Russia, was finally ruined. Fetyukovitch was pleased: it was another godsend. Grushenka’s cross-examination was short, and of course her evidence could hold nothing especially new. She left a very unpleasant impression on the public. Hundreds of scornful eyes followed her as she finished her evidence and sat down again in the courtroom, a good way from Katerina Ivanovna. Mitya said nothing all through her evidence. He sat as though turned to stone, with his eyes on the floor.

For the first moment hardly anyone noticed him come in. The main witnesses, above all the two rival ladies, had already been questioned. For the time being curiosity was satisfied, and the public was almost worn out. Several more witnesses were still to be heard, and after all that had been said they probably had little to add. The time was passing. Ivan walked up with extraordinary slowness. He looked at no one, and he kept his head bowed, as if he were sunk in gloomy thought. His clothes were impeccable, but his face made a painful impression, on me at least. It looked earthy, like the face of a dying man. His eyes were dull. He lifted them and slowly looked around the court. Alyosha jumped up from his seat and moaned, “Ah!” I remember that, but hardly anyone noticed.

“I got it the day before the crime was committed, but he wrote it the day before that, at the tavern—that is, two days before he committed the crime. Look, it’s written on some kind of bill!” she cried breathlessly. “He hated me at that time, because he had behaved contemptibly and was running after that creature ... and because he owed me that three thousand.... Oh! That three thousand humiliated him, because of his own meanness! This is how it came about, that three thousand. I beg you, I implore you, listen to me. Three weeks before he murdered his father, he came to me one morning. I knew he needed money, and I knew what he wanted it for. Yes, yes—to win that creature and carry her off. I knew then that he had been false to me and meant to abandon me. And it was I, I, who gave him that money. I offered it to him on the pretext that he should send it to my sister in Moscow. And as I handed it over, I looked him in the face and said he could send it whenever he liked, ‘in a month’s time would do.’ How, how could he fail to understand that I was practically telling him to his face, ‘You want money to be false to me with your creature, so here is the money. I’m giving it to you myself. Take it, if you have so little honor as to take it!’ I wanted to prove what he was, and what happened? He took it, he took it, and squandered it with that creature in one night.... But he knew, he knew that I knew all about it. I assure you he understood, too, that I gave him that money to test him, to see whether he had lost every scrap of honor and would take it from me. I looked into his eyes and he looked into mine, and he understood it all, and he took it—he carried off my money!”
